title: Capablanca against Marshall: calm defence under a prepared attack
outcomes: Chooses the engine's first move at five moments of a real game before seeing the game move
Reads from the card that, in the engine's depth-16 view, the alternatives tested at 17.hxg4 and 23.Kd3 were rated at least 2.5 and 5 pawns lower
Reads which core skills the game used (a defender's resources, the opponent's best resource, searching for a forced mate)

steps.text:
**New York, 1918.** José Raúl Capablanca (White) met Frank Marshall (Black) in the first round of a Manhattan Chess Club masters tournament. Marshall played the gambit that now carries his name: a pawn for an attack on the king. White won.
You will choose White's moves at five moments. Remarks about the engine name their search depth: they are evidence, not proof.

steps.caption: Marshall (Black) offers a pawn on move 8 and Capablanca (White) takes it. Step through to the first decision.

line.say: White opens with the king's pawn.
White attacks the e5 pawn with the knight.
Black defends it with a knight.
White attacks the defending knight with the bishop.
Black attacks the bishop with a pawn.
Black attacks the e4 pawn with the other knight.
The rook defends the e4 pawn.
Black attacks the bishop again with a pawn.
Black plays d5: the gambit. This pawn is offered.
White takes the e5 pawn with the knight.
The rook takes on e5: White has won a pawn.
Black develops the knight to f6.
The rook goes back to e1.
Black's bishop aims at the h2 pawn.
Black's queen comes to h4; the knight and queen both attack f2.

claims.statement: After 14...Qh4 Black attacks f2 twice (knight and queen).

steps.caption: After 14...Qh4. The game continued with the move you found.

line.say: White plays the d-pawn two squares.
Black takes the f2 pawn with the knight.

claims.statement: After 16...Bg4 the bishop attacks the queen on f3.
At depth 16 the engine rates the position before 15.d4 between 0.00 and 2.25 pawns for White.

steps.caption: After 16...Bg4. White to move; the game went on as follows.

line.say: Black checks with the other bishop.
Black's bishop goes to g3, defending the knight on f2.
The rook takes the knight on f2.
Black's bishop takes the rook on f2.
White develops the bishop to d2.
Black's rook checks along the e-file.

claims.statement: After 22...Rae8+ the rook on e8 attacks the king on e2.
At depth 16 the engine rates the position before 17.hxg4 between 1.00 and 3.25 pawns for White.

steps.caption: After 22...Rae8+. White is in check; the game went on as follows.

line.say: The king steps out of the check.
The queen comes back to f3.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates the position before 23.Kd3 between 1.50 and 3.75 pawns for White.
After 25.Qf3 White defends the queen on f3 1 time(s).

steps.caption: After 25...Qg1. The game went on as follows until move 35.

line.say: The bishop goes to d5, attacking f7.
White takes the c5 pawn with the d-pawn.
Black takes on c3 with the pawn.
The knight takes the pawn on c3.
Black's rook goes to e3, attacking the queen.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates the position before 26.Bd5 between 2.00 and 4.25 pawns for White.

line.say: The bishop takes f7 with check. This is the last move of the score.

claims.statement: White attacks f7 twice (bishop and queen).
At depth 16 the engine rates the position before 36.Bxf7+ between 14.25 and 16.50 pawns for White.

steps.text: **Where was it decided?** In the engine's view (depth 16), the alternatives tested (Qxf2 and Bg5 at move 17; Kf3 and three blocks at move 23) were rated at least 2.5 and 5 pawns lower. Those moves used *A defender's resources*: remove the attacker, and walk the king out of check. The material swung: White won a bishop and a knight, then Black's bishop took a rook on move 20. *The opponent's best resource* means listing the opponent's checks and captures. *Searching for a forced mate* finished it.

steps.prompt: Which moment would you have missed: the quiet d4, taking the bishop with the h-pawn, stepping the king to d3 instead of blocking, the bishop to d5, or the final check? What will you look at first next time a long attack is aimed at your king?

sources: Game score (36 moves, 1-0), checked against each other and replayed move by move with python-chess (every move legal; final position after 36.Bxf7+ is check): (1) Wikipedia 'Ruy Lopez, Marshall Attack' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruy_Lopez,_Marshall_Attack) [S, read through a page-summarising fetch tool]: full 36-move score, but moves 12 to 15 appear in the order 12.d4 Bd6 13.Re1 Ng4 14.h3 Qh4 15.Qf3, which reaches the same position after 15...Nxf2 as the order used here; (2) chesshistory.com 'The Marshall Gambit' (www.chesshistory.com/winter/extra/marshallgambit.html) [S, fetch tool]: moves 8 to 20 in the order used here, mentions 22...Rae8+, 28...Bd6, 35...Re3 and 36.Bxf7+; (3) westernchess.blogspot.com 'Capablanca - Marshall, New York 1918' (2009) [S, fetch tool]: full score in the order used here, but its numbering omits 34.Bxc3 h6 and so ends at 35.Bxf7+; the 36-move numbering (with 34.Bxc3 h6) is the one in sources 1 and 2 and is the only one in which every move is legal.

Event, date and round: ChessBase 'Capablanca vs Marshall Attack, 100 years later' (en.chessbase.com/post/learn-to-play-the-marshall-attack) [S, fetch tool]: first round of the Manhattan Chess Club masters, New York, 23 October 1918; 365chess.com event page lists the game as 1-0, C89. Whether the game ended by resignation or was played on to mate is not settled by what was read; this lesson stops at the last move of the score.
